paras: The Henry County camp-meeting killings were the shooting deaths of seven Black men at a Black camp meeting in Henry County, Alabama, on a night in early September 1888, reportedly Friday, September 7. The killers were described as Milburn, a white man, and his friends, or as masked or unknown white men, and the dead as the supposed ringleaders of an attack on Milburn's house the night before. No arrests had been made when the story ran in papers across the country in the following week.

The camp meeting was held at a Black church near Milburn's residence, and those attending drew their drinking water from his well. On Thursday, with the well nearly dry, Milburn took the bucket away and refused them more water. According to the Washington Critic's version, one man said he would have at least half of the last bucket drawn and started into the house for it, and Milburn shot him in the back of the neck. The New-York Tribune said the man had tried to take the bucket by force and called the wound slight.

That night, by the Tribune's and the Peninsula Enterprise's count, about one hundred of the camp-meeting attendees surrounded Milburn's house and called on him to come out. When he refused, they fired into the house, which the Sun put at over one hundred shots and the Peninsula Enterprise said did no damage, and then left.

The following night a party of white men went to the camp meeting and shot seven men dead. The Tribune said it was 'Milburn and a crowd of his friends', while the Sun spoke of 'a crowd of masked white men' and the Critic of 'a crowd of unknown white men'. The Peninsula Enterprise added that the men were masked, 'supposed to have been Milburn's friends', and that the Black attendees offered no resistance but scattered when the shooting began. None of the dead was named.
The reports of September 9 to 15 all say that no arrests had been made, and no later report of an inquest, arrest or trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached the national press as two separately worded dispatches. A Birmingham special drawn from Eufaula ran on September 10 in the New-York Tribune and the Sun, and a second Birmingham telegram of September 11 appeared in the Washington Critic and was reprinted in Dakota weeklies. A shorter dispatch datelined Hillardsville called the affair 'a fearful battle between whites and blacks' and ran in western dailies on September 11.

Headlines took different lines on the same facts. The Salt Lake Herald headed it 'Butchering Blacks', and Dakota reprints used 'Seven Blacks Killed by a Mob of Whites' and 'Another of Those Mysterious Attacks on Negroes'. The Washington Critic instead headed its account 'They Provoked a Disturbance and Suffered in Consequence', and the Los Angeles Herald ran the Hillardsville text as 'Not the Water of Life', with the dead left 'as a reminder' to the camp.

Weekly digests cut the story to a line or two, and a condensed paragraph in Wilmington and New Jersey papers began with the white men's attack on the camp and gave the attack on Milburn's house as its cause. In Mississippi the Grenada Sentinel ran a brief in its editorial column, without comment, on the seven 'ring leading negroes' killed by 'Milburn and his friends'. The digest line dating a 'battle' at Hillardsville to the 8th ran in weeklies in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Dakota, and the Lebanon Express in Oregon printed the Hillardsville dispatch as late as September 21 under 'Seven Colored Men Killed'.

The papers disagreed on the date: the Eufaula special put the killings on Friday night, while versions of the Hillardsville dispatch said Saturday, the 8th, Sunday or Thursday. The Eufaula special is the fuller account and keeps the same sequence of Thursday shooting, Thursday-night siege and Friday-night killings in every printing. The Willimantic Journal alone placed the killings on the same night as the shooting at the house.

reader.title: Henry County camp-meeting killings
bases: A crowd of white men, described as masked and as Milburn's friends, went to a Black camp meeting at night and shot dead seven men 'supposed to be the ringleaders' of an attack on Milburn's house, outside any legal process (A3, A4, A14).

Two separately worded wire stories, a Birmingham special from Eufaula (A3, A4, A8) and a Hillardsville dispatch (A5, A6), agree that seven Black men were killed by white men after a dispute over a well near a camp meeting, though they differ on the date and on who did the killing.

accounts.gist: Milburn shot a man who tried to take his bucket; about one hundred camp-meeting attendees fired into his house that night; the next night Milburn and his friends, or masked/unknown white men, killed seven supposed ringleaders; no arrests.

accounts.label: Hillardsville dispatch
accounts.gist: A 'fearful battle between whites and blacks' in which a gang 'presumably friends of the white man' visited the camp and 'left seven dead bodies as a reminder' to the rest.

accounts.label: Condensed digest
accounts.gist: White men attacked a camp meeting near Eufaula and killed seven after the negroes had attacked a white man's house over his well.

framing.detail: The Washington Critic headed the Eufaula special 'They Provoked a Disturbance and Suffered in Consequence'.

The Salt Lake Herald called it 'Butchering Blacks' and 'The Latest Race Troubles in the Sunny South' while its text described a 'fearful battle' and the dead as 'a reminder'; the Los Angeles Herald ran the same text as 'Not the Water of Life'.
Most papers ran the wire text without comment, the Sun and the Peninsula Enterprise stressing that no arrests had been made and that the victims offered no resistance.
